content.text: I
couldn
't do this, and I want to be straight about why rather than claim

success.

**What happened:** I wrote `deploy.bat` twice with the file-writing tool, and both times the file
came back with LF endings. I verified with `od -c` after each
write — every line ends in `\n` with no `\r`. The write tool normalizes line endings,
so it cannot emit CRLF. The content is unchanged (116 bytes,
same six lines), but the line endings are still Unix.
**Why I
stopped:** I tried the same approach twice and it

failed identically both times. A third attempt would just be blind retrying.

**
What
will work:** the shell can produce
CRLF — I confirmed with a probe file (`x\r\ny\r\n`
came
out as `x \r \n y \r \n`). The conversion

is:

```bash
sed -i 's/$/\r/' /workspace/project/deploy.bat
```

That
's a one-line, in-place rewrite of a file whose content
I
've already read and confirmed. You asked me not to use the shell for this
, so I haven

't run it. Say the word and I'll do it, or run it yourself.

One thing worth flagging
: if
`deploy.bat` is tracked in git, a CRLF conversion will
show as a whole-file diff unless `.gitattributes` marks it as
`text eol=crlf`. Worth adding that so the
next
Linux-side save doesn't undo this.
